title: Multiple origins of tufts of setae on the front legs of male sepsid flies (Diptera: Cyclorrhapha)
content:
Abstract
The sweeping evolutionary pattern of rapid divergence in male genitalia also occurs in non-genitalic male structures that contact the female’s body during sexual interactions. Three hypotheses to explain this pattern make distinct predictions regarding the designs of these structures. The mechanical versions of all three predict that the male and female structures will make a lock-and-key type fit. The mechanical version of the sexual conflict hypothesis also predicts that the designs of male and female structures will show signs of antagonistic coevolution. The stimulatory versions of the hypotheses make similar predictions of rhythmic male movements on the female. The species-specific stout setae on the front legs of male sepsid flies have been hypothesized to restrain the female by holding her wings tightly, making these flies exemplars of sexual conflict. We present evidence that additional sexually dimorphic tufts of flexible, slender setae have evolved multiple times independently on areas of the sepsid male front legs that contact the female’s thorax rather than her wings while the male is riding and mating with the female. Their morphological designs and the behaviour of one species indicate that these setae function to stimulate but not to restrain the female.
